candidates.summary: The benchmarked handler reads the real wall clock while its fixture pins today=_TODAY, so this benchmark's workload grows with the calendar — a second, unattributed source of the +13.86% that this change does not close and that keeps creeping until 2026-10-17.
candidates.short_summary: progress benchmark's workload grows with wall-clock date
candidates.failure_scenario: perf_db is built with today=date(2026,7,9); test_bench_get_training_plan_progress calls tools.get_training_plan_progress.handler({}), which windows on date.today() (tools.py:3765, :3852-3854 anchor_fwd = max(frontier, today) + 7d). Measured in this checkout against the fixture, on the POST-FIX code: at _TODAY+17d (2026-07-26, the day the committed 0001 baseline was captured on 8edfb70) the serialized payload is 5,447 chars / 11 workouts; at _TODAY+55d (2026-09-02, the CI run the investigation quotes at +13.86%) it is 9,946 chars / 39 workouts; at _TODAY+100d (2026-10-17) it plateaus at 13,869 chars / 56 workouts. Interleaved in-process A/B of the handler across those three frozen dates, 3 rounds x 40 iterations, min: 897.5us / 926.1us / 943.7us — +3.18% at the CI date and +5.15% at plateau versus the baseline-capture date, on identical code. Consequence: the gate reading is part code and part calendar; the fix removes ~6pp of code cost but the remaining drift keeps rising for another six weeks, so 'lands first so the three notes PRs stop inheriting a validate job that is one runner draw from red' is not what this change buys. The diff's own _freeze_progress_clock (tests/test_perf_benchmarks.py:287) documents exactly this mechanism for the count axis and then leaves the latency axis unfrozen.

candidates.summary: The new drift-vs-regression rule (3) asserts that one benchmark out of line with its siblings is necessarily a code regression, but three of the five benchmarks pin `today=_TODAY` and two read the real clock, so the two can diverge from the three with no code change at all.
candidates.short_summary: New CLAUDE.md rule (3) is false for this benchmark suite
candidates.failure_scenario: CLAUDE.md:200-202 now states: 'One benchmark out of line with its four siblings is a code regression however slow the runner was.' In tests/test_perf_benchmarks.py, test_bench_assemble_brief_context (:107), test_bench_build_plan_section (:128) and test_bench_daily_snapshot (:133) all pass `_TODAY.isoformat()` explicitly, while test_bench_get_training_plan_progress (:116) and test_bench_get_training_plan_status (:121) call `handler({})` and window on `date.today()`. The three pinned targets therefore do a fixed amount of work forever; the two unpinned ones do more work every day. Measured above: the progress payload alone grew 5,447 -> 9,946 chars between the baseline-capture date and the CI run quoted as evidence, worth +3.18% on identical code. So the exact shape the rule cites as proof of a code regression (assemble_brief_context -0.34% beside get_training_plan_progress +13.86%) is also the shape calendar drift produces here, and the new rule tells the next reader to stop looking. It is being written into CLAUDE.md as a durable rule, which is where a wrong one costs the most.

candidates.summary: test_the_latency_gate_is_still_armed never asserts that the perf-gate step still passes --benchmark-only, so the single most likely gate demotion — dropping that flag — leaves the test green while the gate silently measures nothing.
candidates.failure_scenario: The test checks only that '--benchmark-compare-fail=min:15%' appears somewhere in .github/workflows/ci.yml and that '--benchmark-skip' appears in pyproject's addopts. pyproject.toml:59 puts --benchmark-skip in the global addopts, so if someone removes `--benchmark-only` from ci.yml's 'Perf-benchmark regression gate' step (.github/workflows/ci.yml:70), addopts skips all six benchmark tests, --benchmark-compare=0001 --benchmark-compare-fail=min:15% compares an empty set, and the step exits 0 forever. Both of this test's assertions still pass. The docstring says 'The failure mode this change could quietly turn into is a gate demotion' — this is the cheapest gate demotion available and the test cannot see it. Same hole for --benchmark-compare=0001 and for the committed .benchmarks/Linux-CPython-3.12-64bit/0001_*.json file existing at all.

    assert "--benchmark-only" in ci
    assert "--benchmark-compare=0001" in ci
    assert "--benchmark-compare-fail=min:15%" in ci
    assert list(root.glob(".benchmarks/Linux-CPython-3.12-64bit/0001_*.json"))

candidates.summary: `assert counts["n"] == 83` pins a payload-shape-derived magic number with no floor/ceiling, so any future field that is a dict or list reddens a perf test for a non-perf reason and the only available fix is hand-editing the number.
candidates.short_summary: == 83 pin reddens on any added dict/list payload field
candidates.failure_scenario: 83 is (number of dicts + number of lists) in the serialized payload at the frozen _TODAY+58d clock — measured 25 at _TODAY, 81 at +56d, 83 at +57d and +58d, 85 at +59d, 115 from +100d. Freezing the clock removes the calendar dependence but not the shape dependence: adding one rollup dict to the response, or one more key whose value is a list, makes the count 84 and turns this test red with a diff that has nothing to do with per-node recursion. The maintainer's cheapest response to a perf test that reddens on unrelated work is to relax it to `<=` or delete it — which is what the r1 findings (f-0583160f, f-7098c483) were trying to prevent in the other direction. A floored range keeps the anti-vacuity property without the toll. The same applies to `== 87` at :312.
